papers.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

papers.title: Cognitive Load modulates the exploration-exploitation trade-off Through Reconfiguration of an IPS-Centered Decision Network
papers.abstract: In dynamic environments where rewards continuously change, adaptive decision-making requires ongoing updates of option-value and uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. This process depends on cognitive resources and involves coordinated interactions among multiple brain regions; however, how cognitive load affects directed exploration in such dynamic environments, and whether these effects are accompanied by changes in interactions among exploration-related brain regions, remains unclear. We embedded a working-memory load manipulation within a dynamic four-armed bandit task. Experiment 1 compared computational models and quantified load-related changes in exploration; Experiment 2 examined these behavioral effects in an independent sample and investigated their neural correlates using fMRI. Across both experiments, high load reduced the uncertainty bonus parameter ({varphi}), indicating weaker directed exploration. Experiment 2 additionally showed lower inverse temperature ({beta}) under high load, indicating more stochastic choices. Directed exploration relative to exploitation more activated the frontopolar cortex (FP), intraparietal sulcus (IPS), anterior insula (aIns), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses indicated stronger functional coupling between the right aIns and IPS under low load. Guided by the candidate connections identified by PPI, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) focused on a three-region subnetwork. Bayesian model selection favored the model with directed-exploration-related input to the IPS, while condition-specific comparisons suggested stronger aIns-to-IPS effective connectivity under low load. Together, these findings link cognitive resource demands to reduced uncertainty-guided directed exploration in a dynamic environment and suggest that this behavioral change is accompanied by selective reconfiguration of interactions within an IPS-centered decision subnetwork.

papers.title: Modified Synchronization Modulation Electric Field attenuates acute brain injury and improves neurological outcomes following stroke induced by transient middle cerebral artery occlusion in rats
papers.abstract: Cerebral ischemia disrupts energy-dependent ion transport and causes acute brain injury. The synchronization modulation electric field (SMEF) platform was developed to support Na+/K+-ATPase function under conditions of limited ATP availability and has shown protective effects in renal ischemia models. We investigated whether cerebral cortical application of third-generation SMEF attenuates cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) for 120 min, with or without SMEF treatment during ischemia. At 24 h after reperfusion, we assessed body-weight change, neurological deficits, open-field locomotor activity, cerebral infarct volume using 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining, hemispheric swelling, and cortical and striatal histopathology. Western blot analysis was performed to measure Na+/K+-ATPase 1, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-{kappa}B) p65 protein abundance. Compared with untreated MCAO rats, SMEF-treated rats exhibited significantly less body-weight loss, lower neurological deficit scores, greater total distance traveled, smaller edema-corrected infarct volumes and percentages, and lower cortical and striatal injury scores. SMEF also shifted Na+/K+-ATPase 1, GFAP, and NF-{kappa}B p65 protein abundance toward sham levels. These findings support an acute protective effect of SMEF following transient MCAO. Further studies should assess Na+/K+-ATPase activity and longer-term functional, histological, and molecular outcomes.

papers.title: Shared and context-dependent cortico-striatal-cerebellar organization of temporal prediction
papers.abstract: Temporal prediction is thought to draw on two subcortical structures: the basal ganglia for the periodic beat, and the cerebellum for the aperiodic interval. Lesion, imaging and electrophysiological studies converge on this division, yet each tests it within a single modality and task, leaving its generality unknown. We developed a battery of timing tasks for multi-task fMRI, densely sampling 31 non-clinical adults in every combination of temporal structure, sensory modality and task. Encoding engaged the same cortico-striatal-cerebellar architecture throughout. Within it, the dorsal striatum was uniquely selective for the production task. Pooled across tasks, it responded more to auditory beat than interval sequences, whereas the cerebellum did not distinguish them. Yet, removing regularity did not lower that response: the preference is for the beat, not for predictability. Temporal prediction therefore draws on a shared architecture whose striatal node is context-dependent: tuned to periodic time, and to time turned into action.

papers.title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
papers.abstract: Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

papers.title: Concurrent neuronal activity gates persistent dendritic spine shrinkage during mGluR-induced long-term depression
papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity is a fundamental mechanism underlying learning and memory. Most excitatory synapses reside on dendritic spines, which undergo both functional and structural changes. These two forms of plasticity are typically tightly coupled: spines enlarge during synaptic strengthening (long-term potentiation, LTP) and shrink during synaptic weakening (long-term depression, LTD). While this coupling is well established for NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent LTD, there are conflicting reports concerning whether spine shrinkage is coupled with metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD. To investigate the source of these conflicting results, we induced mGluR-LTD with the mGluR1/5 agonist DHPG in organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures and monitored changes in spine morphology and calcium transients in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing DsRed2 and GCaMP6. We found that mGluR activation is accompanied by long-term spine shrinkage only under conditions of elevated hippocampal neuronal activity. This form of plasticity, mGluR-induced neuronal activity-dependent structural LTD (MIND-sLTD), requires mGluR1/5 activation and de novo protein synthesis, but not NMDAR signaling. Persistent structural changes occur only when neuronal activity coincides temporally with mGluR activation. MIND-sLTD also occurs at individual synapses: mGluR activation induces persistent single-spine shrinkage only when synchronized with two-photon glutamate uncaging, independently of NMDARs. These findings identify a novel form of structural plasticity and suggest a coincidence-detection mechanism that integrates mGluR signaling with synaptic activity to consolidate long-term spine remodeling.

papers.title: Voluntary control of human motor units is more flexible in facial than limb muscles
papers.abstract: Facial expressions require different motor circuits than those controlling the limbs. How the motor system uses flexible neural control across muscles innervated by the brainstem versus the spinal cord is unclear. Using intramuscular and surface electromyography in human participants performing low-effort, sustained voluntary contractions, we show that brainstem motor units function with more features of flexible control compared to motor units in several spinally innervated muscles. Individual motor units recorded from the frontalis muscle (brainstem-innervated) used a wider range of regular and irregular firing rates, reflecting both greater independence and higher input sensitivity than spinal-innervated motor units. When assessing motor unit pairs, we again found that brainstem control relied more heavily on features corresponding to independent inputs relative to spinal control. Voluntary control of brainstem-innervated muscle therefore used more flexible neural strategies than the control of upper and lower limb muscles we tested. These findings support an anatomical hypothesis for adaptive neural control, in which the degree of independent motor unit activation is constrained by how muscles are accessed across cortex.

papers.title: Computational model for Rumination as Self-Supervised Learning in a World Model
papers.abstract: Rumination is a cognitive process characterized by repetitive negative thoughts that persist even in the absence of external threats. Although excessive rumination is associated with stress-related mental disorders, the computational mechanisms underlying its persistence and its impact on threat perception remain unclear. Here, we propose a computational framework in which rumination emerges from recursive learning within a world model. Inspired by the social defeat stress (SDS) paradigm in mice, our model assumes that direct experiences of social defeat first establish beliefs about the threat posed by an aggressor. These beliefs subsequently generate internally simulated experiences, which are repeatedly used to update the beliefs themselves. We investigated how this recursive process reshapes threat perception by allowing the rumination gain, a learning rate controlling internal belief updating, to take both positive and negative values. Through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis, we found that positive gains did not simply reinforce acquired threat beliefs, while negative gains did not simply erase them. Instead, both positive and negative gains could generate markedly divergent threat perceptions, with some simulated individuals perceiving severe threats and others perceiving almost none, despite identical initial beliefs and external experiences. These outcomes qualitatively resemble the coexistence of stress-susceptible and resilient mice following SDS. Our findings suggest that rumination is not merely a repetition of past experiences but a self-referential learning process that can transform identical stressful experiences into fundamentally different perceptions of threat.

papers.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
papers.abstract: Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

papers.title: Reduced bushy cell firing limits binaural coding after cochlear synaptopathy
papers.abstract: Listeners can experience difficulties with spatial hearing and speech understanding in complex acoustic environments despite near-normal hearing thresholds. Cochlear synaptopathy, which reduces auditory nerve input without elevating thresholds, is one candidate mechanism, but how this peripheral deafferentation disrupts binaural processing remains unclear. We adapted a physiologically constrained computational model incorporating the auditory periphery, spherical and globular bushy cells of the cochlear nucleus and the lateral superior olive (LSO) to examine the separate and combined effects of reduced afferent input and degraded spike timing. Synaptopathy was modeled as loss of auditory nerve inputs to bushy cells, whereas central myelin dysfunction was modeled as increased temporal jitter in bushy cell outputs. Loss of auditory nerve input substantially reduced bushy cell firing rates without degrading phase locking. Despite this preserved temporal precision, binaural tuning in the LSO declined disproportionately, where moderate afferent loss produced substantial reductions in sensitivity to interaural envelope phase differences. In contrast, temporal jitter preserved bushy cell firing rates but degraded phase locking and binaural tuning. Selective loss of input to excitatory versus inhibitory pathways produced opposite changes in overall LSO firing rate, yet both reduced binaural interaction. These results identify two mechanistically distinct routes to impaired binaural coding: too few precisely timed spikes, and a sufficient number of spikes arriving with inadequate temporal precision. These results predict that correcting myelin-related timing deficits alone would leave substantial binaural coding impairment when cochlear deafferentation persists, motivating interventions that address both diminished afferent drive and impaired transmission.

papers.title: Substitution and Concomitant Distractor Intrusions Reveal Different Neural Dynamics of Temporal Selection
papers.abstract: Selective attention requires target identification and exclusion of irrelevant information. We distinguished substitution and concomitant distractor intrusions in 29 adults performing rapid serial visual presentation with uncertain target number. Substitution reports, in which only the distractor was reported, showed an attenuated and delayed N2 posterior contralateral (N2pc) component and a smaller P3b; intrusion probability decreased with target-distractor numerical distance. Concomitant reports included both identities without reliable differences in measured averaged event-related potentials from correct reports of the same sequence. However, target-first concomitant reports were distinguishable through distributed activity and showed reduced left-frontal power, predominantly in theta. Comparisons with correct single- and dual-target reports indicated that reporting two identities did not simply reproduce genuine two-target processing. These findings distinguish processing profiles of substitution and concomitant intrusions and extend temporal-selection accounts from attentional engagement to subsequent regulation of which processed identities enter report.

papers.title: Lipidomic Profiling of L1CAM+ Extracellular Vesicles in Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) lacks minimally invasive biomarkers that reflect neuron-derived molecular alterations. Here, we performed a pilot study for untargeted Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS)-based lipidomics on serum total extracellular vesicles (tEVs) and L1CAM-enriched EVs (L1CAM+EVs) in patients with PD and healthy controls (n=10 per group; N=40). Partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) separated PD from control samples in both fractions L1CAM+EVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.879; tEVs: R2Y = 0.998, Q2 = 0.876), and distinguished L1CAM+EVs from tEVs within PD samples (R2Y = 0.999, Q2 = 0.925). In PD tEVs, triacylglycerols, fatty acids, phosphatidylcholines, sphingomyelins and phosphatidylserines were increased, and pathway analysis indicated enhanced conversion of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) to phosphatidylserine (PS). In contrast, PD L1CAM+EVs showed increased DG, LPA and PS with reduced LPC; pathway reconstruction indicated enhanced PE-PC-DG and LPC-PC flux with reduced de novo PC and SM synthesis. Within PD, L1CAM+EVs were depleted of multiple sphingomyelin species (e.g., SM 41:2;O3, SM 35:2;O3, SM 41:3;O3) and glycerophospholipids relative to tEVs, whereas SPB 18:0;O2 and FA 16:4 were relatively enriched. These findings indicate that L1CAM-enriched EVs carry a PD-associated lipid signature that is qualitatively distinct from that of controls, supporting their evaluation as a complementary source of neuron-related lipid biomarkers.

papers.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
papers.abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices--signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set--into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time-frequency decomposition including the delta band (2-4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

papers.title: Tensor decomposition for data-driven analysis of OP-MEG: a feasibility study
papers.abstract: Optically Pumped Magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OP-MEG) enables flexible, close-to-scalp recordings unlocking access to new patient cohorts and naturalistic paradigms. The data collected during OP-MEG sessions is naturally multi-dimensional, often containing information across patients, trials, conditions, space, frequency and time which can be stored in tensors. Canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) is an unsupervised method that separates multidimensional data into components with linked spatial, spectral and temporal profiles. This allows neural responses to be characterised across brain regions, frequency and time simultaneously,without specifying these features in advance. This makes CPD well suited to OP-MEG data, where signals naturally vary across these dimensions. Here, we applied CPD to whole-brain, source-reconstructed OP-MEG data from three participants with epilepsy during a simple visuomotor task, modelling neural activity jointly across brain regions, frequency and time. We split these subject-specific tensors into event-related power decrease and increase (referred to as ERD and ERS for convenience) tensors so that a more interpretable and computationally efficient non-negative CPD variant could be applied. CPD paired with consensus clustering on spatio-spectral-temporal networks successfully identified cross-patient, simultaneous motor beta and visual alpha suppression. Permutation-based null distribution tests were used to exclude tensors that lacked significant low-rank structure. These findings demonstrate the applicability of tensor decompositions to electrophysiological data as the pipeline recovers canonical visuomotor responses without prespecifying region, band or latency.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
papers.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how recurrent circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our results highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscillations at the stimulation frequency.

papers.title: NeuroMetaBench: Expert-curated benchmark for evaluating automated neuroimaging meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis is widely used to generate hypotheses and interpret findings, reducing the time and effort required for manual literature searches and evidence curation. However, how closely these methods recover effortful expert-curated syntheses has not been established. We present NeuroMetaBench, an openly available benchmark linking expert curation records across stages of systematic review, from author-stated eligibility criteria and research-article inclusion decisions to individual analysis selections and meta-analysis-specific reference maps. The resource includes bibliographic records for 1,611 research-article inclusions across 17 quantitative review articles and candidate search pools for three. For nine review articles, it also provides analysis-level selections and coordinate data across 35 meta-analyses, documenting which reported results contributed to each meta-analysis and enabling reproducible construction of standardized reference maps. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating three established automated methods: Neurosynth, NeuroQuery, and NeuroVLM. Across the benchmark, automated maps generally showed limited to moderate spatial correspondence with expert-curated reference maps, with substantial variation across meta-analysis topics and characteristics. NeuroMetaBench provides an openly available, community-driven resource for evaluating established automated meta-analysis methods, and is well positioned to evaluate emerging LLM-based approaches to automated neuroimaging synthesis.

papers.title: Conditioned expectations drive false odor detection
papers.abstract: Research in auditory and visual fields has shown that false percepts can emerge when perceptual priors outweigh incoming sensory information. However, the role of similar top-down mechanisms in generating false percepts in the olfactory domain is less understood. To address this, we implemented a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm in which we first individually determined the odor detection thresholds of Butanol (n = 55) using an adaptive algorithm. Participants then completed an odor detection task where on each trial one of two distinct visual cues was paired with either a supra-threshold, threshold, or sub-threshold concentration of Butanol, or no odor. In the first three trial blocks, one visual stimulus (strong cue) was paired more frequently with supra-threshold concentrations, and the other visual stimulus (weak cue) was paired more frequently with sub-threshold concentrations. In the last three blocks both cues were paired most frequently with the no odor condition. We observed significantly greater odor detection rates on no odor trials for the strong cue compared to the weak cue. Importantly, this finding could not be explained by differences in total number of visual cue presentations or other task variables. Further, the difference in odor detection rate for the strong and weak cues during the supra-threshold conditioning trials predicted the difference in false odor detection during the no odor trials, suggesting that the prior formed between the strong cue and odor contributed to the false olfactory percepts. This demonstrates that false odor perception can be enhanced by the expectation of an olfactory stimulus in a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm. These findings could yield therapeutic insight into the mechanisms underlying pathological olfactory hallucinations.

papers.title: RhoA Overexpression in Nucleus Accumbens-to-Ventral Tegmental Area Spiny Projection Neurons Induces Negative Affective-like Behavior
papers.abstract: Rationale. Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is increasingly affecting populations worldwide and becoming a leading cause of psychological disabilities. However, MDD patients do not respond to current medications, resulting in treatment resistance. This situation demands more basic research to identify targetable molecules and the specific brain circuits and cell types that underlie negative affective pathology. Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) mediates negative affective-like behaviors via dendritic atrophy of nucleus accumbens (NAc) D1 (dopamine receptor 1)-Spiny Projection Neurons (SPNs), making RhoA a promising target for new depression therapeutics. However, the sufficiency of RhoA elevation in NAc projection-specific D1-SPNs is yet to be investigated. Objectives. Whether RhoA overexpression selectively in NAc-to-ventral tegmental area (VTA) SPNs (NAc-VTA SPNs) is sufficient to induce negative affective-like behavior. Whether chronic stress (CS) induces RhoA mRNA expression in this specific projection. Methods. A retrograde (Rg) vector expressing Cre recombinase was infused into the VTA together with Cre-dependent vectors overexpressing either a control expressing only enhanced Yellow Fluorescent Protein (eYFP) or RhoA-eYFP in NAc-VTA neurons. Mice then underwent a battery of affective assays (social interaction, etc.) and a two-choice sucrose operant task assessing motivation. RNA in situ hybridization (RHA-ish) quantified RhoA mRNA in NAc-VTA D1-SPNs of chronically stressed versus unstressed (control) mice. Results. RhoA overexpression in NAc-VTA SPNs, which are primarily D1-SPNs, elicited negative affective-like phenotypes, including social avoidance, reduced open-arm exploration, decreased grooming, and increased latency to approach food. RhoA and control groups acquired a food operant task similarly. However, RhoA overexpression significantly reduced operant responding and breakpoint during progressive-ratio testing. RhoA overexpression in the NAc-VTA projection neurons also diminished persistent sucrose-seeking behavior. Chronic stress induced RhoA mRNA expression selectively in NAc-VTA neurons.

papers.title: Cross- species developmental multiomics identifies RHOJ as a regulator of human-enriched cortical progenitor states
papers.abstract: Expansion of the primate cerebral cortex is associated with increased proliferation and diversification of neural progenitors, particularly outer radial glia (oRG), but the evolutionary developmental changes underlying these features remain unclear. Here, we integrate time-resolved, paired single-nucleus transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiles from human, macaque and mouse fetal cortex to compare their radial glial developmental programs. Developmental alignment within a conserved corticogenic framework identified two human-enriched programs associated with oRG features and progenitor maintenance. We identified RHOJ, which encodes a conserved small GTPase, as an oRG-enriched gene with elevated expression in human cortex. Ectopic RHOJ expression in mouse fetal cortex increased the proportions of neural progenitors and cells with oRG-like morphology, and altered the relative abundance of SATB2+ and TBR1+ neuronal populations. An intronic RHOJ enhancer showed greater reporter activity for the human sequence than for orthologous non-human primate sequences, partly attributable to a human-specific substitution within a predicted AP-1 binding motif. In human cortical organoids, deletion of this enhancer reduced RHOJ expression, impaired organoid growth and altered progenitor and neuronal populations. These findings link human-enriched developmental programs to evolutionary modification of progenitor properties, supporting altered deployment of conserved genes as a potential contributor to cortical progenitor diversification.

papers.title: Glial involvement in mitochondrial metabolic alterations in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Metabolic alterations in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) emerge early in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their molecular and cellular basis remains unclear. We hypothesized that impaired glial energy metabolism, particularly mitochondrial oxidative metabolism in astrocytes, underlies the metabolic vulnerability of the PCC in AD. To test this hypothesis, we integrated human PCC proteomics and transcriptomics with magnetic resonance spectroscopy in AppNL-G-F knock-in (APP-KI) mice. Human proteomic and transcriptomic analyses converged on reduced mitochondrial oxidative-metabolism signatures associated with AD pathology and cognition. APP-KI hippocampus showed proteomic and 1H-MRS alterations resembling those in the human AD PCC. Spatial transcriptomics identified widespread metabolic transcriptional changes and reduced mitochondrial pathway signatures in glia-enriched hippocampal clusters. Hyperpolarized [1-13C]pyruvate spectroscopy showed reduced bicarbonate labelling in APP-KI mice, consistent with impaired oxidative pyruvate metabolism. These findings reveal convergent mitochondrial alterations in human AD and APP-KI mice, implicating glial cells, particularly astrocytes, in the associated dysfunction.

papers.title: TSC/mTORC1-dependent proteostasis in stress-recruited prefrontal ensembles gates flexible avoidance
papers.abstract: Adaptive threat responses require accurate appraisal of danger signals and flexible behavioral control. Anxiety and trauma-related disorders are marked by avoidance that outlasts the circumstances warranting it, yet such states rarely arise from genetic or environmental insult alone. Here we show that the two converge on a defined prefrontal population by releasing the TSC complex's constitutive brake on mTORC1. Using activity-dependent genetic targeting in mice, we accessed medial prefrontal cortex neurons recruited during the early phase of social isolation - a population projecting predominantly to the lateral septum - and deleted Tsc2 selectively within them. Ensemble-specific Tsc2 haploinsufficiency suppressed autophagic flux without altering bulk translation and produced behavioral avoidance that was rapid and efficient yet no longer under stimulus control, escalating into extra-CS epochs and generalizing to a novel, non-reinforced context. Mutant animals bypassed the phase in which freezing and shuttling compete, and in vivo calcium fiber photometry revealed ensembles locked to the cue but unable to signal trial outcome or track the competing Pavlovian response. Reinstating restraint on mTORC1 through ensemble-restricted Raptor knockdown or systemic Rapamycin restored stimulus control over avoidance, whereas Tsc2 haploinsufficiency in mPFC neurons without social isolation produced no phenotype. These findings identify TSC-restrained, mTORC1-dependent proteostasis within stress-recruited ensembles as a gene-by-environment locus for maladaptive avoidance. More broadly, they suggest that excessive avoidance in anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders may arise not from genetic risk or adversity alone but from their convergence on mTORC1 signaling cascade.

papers.title: Distinct effects of aging and hearing loss on mouse auditory cortex
papers.abstract: Age-related hearing loss is accompanied by changes in auditory cortical activity, but it remains unclear which changes reflect aging itself and which depend on the loss of peripheral input. Here we compared spontaneous and sound-evoked activity in the auditory cortex of awake C57BL/6J (C57) mice, which develop early-onset hearing loss, with that of C57BL/6J x CBA/Ca F1 hybrid mice, which retain their hearing. In both strains, aging increased the irregularity of spontaneous firing and reduced the spike-timing precision of narrow-spiking neurons during natural sound presentation. In C57 mice, aging was additionally associated with a greater loss of sound-responsive neurons, increased spontaneous firing of broad-spiking neurons and more variable sound-evoked spike trains. At the level of individual neurons, the effect of sound on contrast entropy, a firing-rate-normalized measure of spike-pattern diversity, also diverged between strains with age and became negative in middle-aged and old C57's neurons. Nevertheless, population activity discriminated spontaneous, natural sound-evoked and noise-evoked conditions with high accuracy at every age in both strains. Thus, aging and hearing loss have distinct effects on the spiking of individual auditory cortical neurons, whereas population activity continues to discriminate sound conditions.

papers.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

papers.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
papers.abstract: Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

papers.title: Modulation of genetic- and toxicant-induced Parkinson's disease outcomes by SV2C in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Several proteins involved in dopaminergic neurotransmission have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), including synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2C (SV2C). At least seven SNPs in SV2C are associated with PD, including variants that modify: PD risk, PD risk in GBA carriers, PD severity, contribution of environmental factors (e.g., nicotine) to PD, and PD patient response to L-DOPA and dopamine therapies. Although the specific function of SV2C remains unknown, there is significant evidence supporting a role of SV2C in mediating vesicular dopamine content, vesicular trafficking, and neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, SV2C directly associates with -synuclein and mediates the content of neurotoxicants within synaptic vesicles. Taken together, these data suggest that SV2C plays a critical role in mediating PD risk and pathogenesis. To investigate whether SV2C mediates PD outcomes, transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) expressing human SV2C, human -synuclein, or both, were exposed to the PD-associated neurotoxicants 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+), rotenone, and paraquat, and evaluated for PD outcomes including lethality and dopamine-mediated motor behavior. Although SV2C-expressing C. elegans showed a shorter lifespan at baseline, SV2C expression conferred organism-level protection against MPP+ and paraquat-induced lethality. While -synuclein expression exacerbated lethality following MPP+ and paraquat exposure, SV2C provided partial rescue of lethality in -synuclein-expressing C. elegans. However, no differences in lethality were observed based on genotype following rotenone exposure. Interestingly, sublethal toxicant exposure did not reveal a protective effect of SV2C expression on motor behavior for any of the toxicants. To determine whether SV2C's modulation of vesicular uptake mediated the protection against lethality from PD-associated neurotoxicants observed in C. elegans, in vitro assays of vesicular dopamine uptake dynamics were performed. SV2C expression resulted in a protective shift in toxicant-induced uptake inhibition following MPP+ and rotenone exposure; however, there was no paraquat-induced inhibition of vesicular uptake observed in vitro. Taken together, these data suggest that while SV2C plays a protective role in mediating organism-level survival in C. elegans following MPP+ and paraquat exposure, the mechanisms of protection and the role of SV2C in modulating vesicular dopamine dynamics and dopamine-mediated behaviors following toxicant exposure require further analysis. Future studies can evaluate additional PD outcomes in these exposure models and investigate SV2C-mediated mechanisms of protection such as regulation of neurotransmitter handling and oxidative stress.

papers.title: Mechanical strain and strain rate define thresholds of single-cell and ensemble calcium disruption in traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Mechanically induced brain injury triggers rapid cellular responses that shape long-term neurological outcomes, yet the early evolution of functional network disruption remains poorly defined. In particular, how neuronal activity changes within seconds of deformation and whether these responses determine subsequent circuit organization remain unknown. Here, we combined controlled mechanical stretch with high-speed calcium imaging to measure neuronal calcium dynamics within seconds of injury and track the same cells over 24 hours. We identify strain- and strain-rate-dependent disruption modes, including rapid reduction of calcium transient activity under moderate loading and collapse of network bursting beyond distinct mechanical thresholds. These disruptions persist despite preserved cell viability, revealing an additional functional injury pathway. These findings show that functional impairment emerges within seconds of mechanical loading and that the severity of deformation dictates the mode of network disruption, establishing mechanical thresholds as key determinants of secondary injury progression.

papers.title: Perineuronal net homeostasis by the NRG1/ErbB4 signaling for cognitive function
papers.abstract: Perineuronal nets (PNN) is the specialized extracellular matrix that enwraps the soma and proximal dendrites of neurons in particular interneurons. During neural development, PNN expression marks the closure of the critical period of visual cortical development. The roles of PNN in the adult brain and how its expression is regulated remain less understood. Here we show that enriched environment (EE) increases PNN in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in adult mice with improved cognitive functions. Analysis of snRNA-seq data of EE and control PFC identified the neuregulin1 (NRG1)/ErbB4 signaling as the pathway to regulate PNN expression. Ablation of ErbB4 or acute chemical genetic inhibition of its kinase activity reduced PNN and impaired cognitive function and prevented the promotion effect of EE. The expression of PNN and the core component aggrecan (ACAN) was increased in cultured interneurons stimulated with NRG1. ACAN mutation abolished PNN, weakened excitatory inputs and intrinsic excitability of ErbB4+ interneurons, and impaired cognitive functions. ACAN could undergo liquid-liquid phase separation to form condensates alone or together with other proteoglycans of the PNN. Finally, we demonstrate that restoring ACAN could ameliorate PNN and cognitive deficits in ErbB4 mutant mice. These results suggest that EE may improve cognitive functions by enhancing NRG1/ErbB4 signaling to increase PNN levels, identifying a signaling pathway critical to PNN homeostasis in adult animals

papers.title: Investigating Motor Skill Acquisition in Mice and Humans: Towards A Cross-Species Paradigm
papers.abstract: Relating non-invasive observations of human brain plasticity to cellular processes identified in animal models remains a major challenge in neuroscience. We address this challenge by introducing a paradigm for studying motor skill acquisition across species. We designed a human chopstick grasping task modeled after the rodent single-pellet reaching task, resulting in a comparable sequence of reach-to-grasp movements across species. We studied 48 young adult male C57BL/6N mice and 71 young men, comparing trained groups with untrained controls. In both mice and humans, structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before, during, and after motor training. The functional form of behavioral performance gains on the trained task was highly similar across species. In trained compared to control mice, analysis of the early learning interval revealed decreases in regional volume in contralateral primary motor and forelimb somatosensory cortices, with greater volume reductions in primary motor cortex associated with better reaching performance. In humans, performance gains transferred to other chopstick tasks but not to general dexterity, and no reliable changes in gray matter volume were observed. Quantitative MRI, however, revealed early training-related changes in tissue-sensitive measures, including increases in magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) and longitudinal relaxation rate (R1) in contralateral motor and frontal regions, potentially reflecting an increase in intracortical myelin. Thus, early structural changes in the contralateral motor cortex were detected in both species, but the degree to which these changes reflect a common biological mechanism is unclear. We conclude that the present cross-species paradigm provides a viable starting point for studying brain plasticity across species. Future work needs to relate macroscopic structural changes more directly to cellular processes by applying longitudinal microscopic imaging and MRI in the same animals.

papers.title: Reduced subcortical envelope phase locking in middle age without detectable changes in perceptual discrimination
papers.abstract: Cochlear synaptopathy (CS) can occur during normal aging without elevated audiometric thresholds and has been hypothesized to contribute to suprathreshold auditory difficulties. Frequency-following responses (FFRs) have been proposed as markers of CS, but whether their envelope- and temporal-fine-structure-related components are similarly affected by age, and whether such changes relate to perceptual sensitivity, remains unclear. Here, we examined associations between age-related FFR changes and perceptual sensitivity in young (n = 20, 19-32 years) and middle-aged (n = 20, 40-58 years) adults with clinically normal hearing. Participants completed psychoacoustic discrimination tasks for formant frequency, formant bandwidth, and temporal-envelope shape using stationary stimuli in quiet and background noise. FFRs were recorded using dynamic stimuli varying along the same acoustic dimensions. We quantified envelope- and temporal-fine-structure-related phase locking (PLVENV and PLVTFS) across harmonics and assessed how it tracked stimulus changes over time. Mean PLVENV decreased significantly with age, and PLVENV tracking of decreasing formant bandwidth and temporal-envelope shape weakened with age. In contrast, mean PLVTFS and temporal slopes of PLVTFS spectral centroid were not significantly associated with age. Discrimination thresholds showed no significant associations with age, either in quiet or in noise, and PLV measures did not significantly explain individual differences in discrimination thresholds. These findings indicate that age-related reductions in subcortical envelope phase locking can be detected by middle age without corresponding measurable reductions in perceptual sensitivity.

papers.title: Intranasal oxytocin increases early tactile engagement with a robotic dog: A within-session effect without consolidation
papers.abstract: Oxytocin (OXT) is centrally involved in mammalian affiliation, but whether it modulates affiliative behavior toward artificial social agents, and how such an effect unfolds within a single interaction, is unclear. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled study, 61 healthy adult males received 40 IU intranasal OXT or PLA before interacting with a Sony aibo robotic dog across an initial free interaction, a cooperative task-learning phase, and a final free interaction, with ten affiliative behaviors coded from video. OXT increased tactile engagement early: participants touched aibo longer during the initial free interaction, the only outcome of ten to survive family-wise correction. A weaker increase in smile frequency did not survive correction, and instrumental behavior was unaffected. Contrary to our second prediction, the advantage was not consolidated: it held through the initial interaction, closed across the intervening task, and was absent at the final one. An exploratory decomposition located the effect: participants under OXT did not initiate contact more often, and the difference was carried by how long each episode of contact was sustained. Urinary OXT confirmed group-level exposure. Because the design included no comparison condition and confounded interaction period with elapsed time and pharmacokinetics, it cannot establish bond formation, robot specificity, or consolidation as a psychological process. What it does bound is where and when OXT acted: on the maintenance of contact rather than its initiation, and only while the agent was novel, a pattern that fits salience- and novelty-based accounts better than bond formation.
